title: Documents Into Guides, Five Stages Deep
description: A multi-stage document-to-HTML conversion pipeline: drag-and-drop upload, topic grouping, staged processing with progress tracking, error recovery, concurrent batches, and rate limiting that keeps external APIs alive.

lines.text: Customer success team has fifty PDFs needing HTML guides by tomorrow. Manual conversion: two days of copy-paste.
Or a script.
Or a pipeline that groups topics, converts, shows progress, recovers from failures, handles rate limits. This project builds exactly that.
Why not just send all fifty PDFs to ChatGPT in one batch?
Context window limits, rate limits, no progress visibility, and no recovery from individual failures.
The pipeline exists because naive batching breaks at scale.

sections.title: Why five stages instead of one?

lines.text: Pipeline stages per document: upload validation, text extraction, topic classification, content transformation, HTML rendering.
One monolithic call means failure at stage four restarts everything, wasting tokens and time.
Staged processing resumes from last checkpoint.
What does each stage do?
Stage one checks file type, size, readability. Stage two extracts raw text. Stage three sends batch to OpenAI for topic grouping.
Stage four transforms individual docs into structured content. Stage five renders final HTML.
Tech stack: Next.js frontend for drag-and-drop UI, FastAPI backend for orchestration, OpenAI for transformation.
Docker Compose packages everything for reproducible startup.
Five stages sounds like a lot of engineering for converting documents.
Each stage earns its existence by enabling targeted retry and checkpoint recovery.
Documents process concurrently in bounded batches. Not fifty parallel; that trips the limiter.
Rate limiting: ten uploads per minute enforced server-side. Prevents overload and runaway cost.
Error recovery: failed document marks itself, others finish independently. Retry button targets only failures.
Duplicate detection hashes file contents. Re-upload returns cached result without spending tokens.
Progress reporting? Polling. Frontend checks percentage every few seconds. Each stage transition increments count.
WebSockets nicer but polling simpler and sufficient.
Upload validation stage checks file extension, size limit, and attempts basic readability probe.
A corrupted PDF passes extension check but fails readability. Better to catch here than waste tokens downstream.
Text extraction uses PyPDF2 or python-docx depending on file type. Output is plain text with page markers preserved.
Topic classification sends all extracted texts to OpenAI in one call. Model groups them into categories.
Grouping prompt asks for JSON output mapping document IDs to topic labels.
Content transformation runs per-document. Prompt converts raw text into structured guide sections.
HTML rendering takes structured output and wraps it in styled templates. Pure Python templating, no additional LLM call.
Concurrency managed by asyncio semaphore limiting parallel OpenAI calls to three.
Rate limiter tracks upload timestamps in sliding window. Eleventh upload within sixty seconds gets four-two-nine response.
Twelve files dragged onto upload zone: six PDFs, four Word docs, two images.
Images rejected immediately with clear message. Ten proceed.
Extraction succeeds for nine. One scanned PDF has no text layer, flags unreadable.
Topic grouping sends nine texts in one OpenAI batch call, sorts into three topics.
Transformation runs concurrently, three at a time. Eight succeed, one times out.
Rendering produces all eight guides. User retries failed transformation. Second attempt succeeds.
Detailed walkthrough of processing twelve mixed files.
User drops files onto browser zone. Frontend sends multipart form to backend endpoint.
Backend validates each: two image files rejected immediately with clear error message returned to frontend.
Ten valid files enter pipeline. Upload validation assigns unique job IDs and stores metadata in SQLite.
Text extraction runs synchronously for each. Nine succeed. One scanned PDF yields empty string, flagged unreadable.
Nine extracted texts batch-sent to OpenAI for topic grouping. Response sorts into three topics: setup guides, troubleshooting, release notes.
Content transformation launches concurrently with semaphore limiting to three simultaneous OpenAI calls.
Eight transformations succeed within timeout. One times out after sixty seconds and marks failed.
HTML rendering converts eight structured outputs into styled pages organized under topic headings.
Frontend polls status endpoint every three seconds. Progress bar advances as stages complete.
Final state: eight complete, one extraction failure, one transformation failure. User clicks retry on transformation failure only. Succeeds.
Average doc: three thousand words, four thousand tokens extracted.
OpenAI transformation per doc: eight thousand tokens including output.
Twelve documents cost roughly one dollar with GPT-four-mini.
Transformation takes five to fifteen seconds per document. Concurrent batches of three mean ten docs finish in forty seconds.
Rate limit keeps within OpenAI tier-one thresholds comfortably.
Resource consumption measured during testing.
Average document: three thousand words, four thousand tokens extracted.
Topic grouping call: nine documents totaling thirty-six thousand tokens input, five hundred tokens output.
Per-document transformation: four thousand tokens input plus four thousand output average.
GPT-four-mini pricing: input sixty cents per million, output two dollars forty per million.
Total cost for twelve documents: approximately seventy cents. Well within reasonable take-home budget.
Wall-clock time: extraction instant, grouping call five seconds, transformation batches forty seconds total, rendering instant.
End-to-end for ten documents: under one minute.
Drag-and-drop frontend to FastAPI backend. Upload validation filters immediately.
Text extraction pulls raw content. Topic grouping via single LLM call across batch.
Concurrent transformation in bounded batches with retry support. Rendering organizes by topic.
Duplicates skip via hashing. Failures mark individually. Progress polling throughout.
Complete pipeline flow once more.
Drag-and-drop uploads to FastAPI. Validation filters bad files. Extraction pulls text.
Single LLM call groups topics across batch. Concurrent transformation with semaphore. HTML rendering organizes by topic.
Progress polling updates UI. Duplicate detection via content hash prevents wasted tokens on re-uploads.
Four-twenty-nine rate limit response mid-batch. Burst of transformation failures. Fix exponential backoff with jitter.
PDF uses embedded fonts with no text mapping. Garbled extraction. Fix detect low confidence, suggest OCR.
Browser closes mid-processing. Orphaned jobs consume quota. Fix background runner with timeout cleanup.
Pending: max file size? Who pays tokens at scale? Editable HTML before publish? Simultaneous duplicate uploads?
Additional failure modes observed or anticipated.
OpenAI returns four-two-nine rate limit during concurrent transformation burst.
Signal: multiple failures cluster together. Fix exponential backoff with jitter rather than immediate retry.
PDF uses non-standard font encoding producing garbled extraction output.
Signal: transformation produces nonsensical guide content. Fix detect garbled text heuristically and flag for manual review.
Browser closes during long processing. Background tasks orphaned.
Signal: jobs stuck in in-progress indefinitely consuming quota. Fix background task runner with timeout and periodic cleanup.
Pending: max supported file size? Token billing responsibility? Editable HTML output? Concurrent duplicate upload handling?
Stage four fails for one doc: others unaffected?
Same file re-upload returns cached result without spending tokens?
Progress reflects actual transitions or fake elapsed time?
Fourth: if OpenAI goes down entirely, does the system fail gracefully or lose in-flight work?
Fifth: can you add a sixth processing stage without modifying existing stages?
Self-test: same PDF uploaded twice with different filenames. Duplicate or distinct? Why?
Next time: natural language to SQL where the model writes code touching production data.
What about versioning? User uploads revision of same document.
Content hash differs on revision so treated as new. Version tracking would need document-level identity beyond content hash.
